summary:
We developed the "Young Astronaut Mission Training Tool"—an interactive, zero-install planetary habitat simulator that puts students directly in command of Artemis (Moon) and Ares (Mars) outposts.

Most space STEM tools either oversimplify engineering trade-offs into trivial games or overwhelm young learners with dense, inaccessible formulas. We solved this by turning authentic aerospace physics into intuitive, real-time cause-and-effect systems. Students must balance competing life-or-death demands: ECLSS life support (oxygen and water recycling), radiation shielding, power grids, and hydroponic agriculture. When a Martian dust storm hits, they experience firsthand why critical decisions make or break a mission.

This project matters because it cultivates systems-thinking and problem-solving in the Artemis Generation. Furthermore, its 100% offline standalone design guarantees that any classroom worldwide—regardless of hardware budget or internet access—can freely explore deep space engineering.
details:
Project Details:

1. What Does It Do & How Does It Work?

"Young Astronaut: Moon & Mars Mission Training Tool" is an interactive, browser-based aerospace engineering simulation designed to empower young students to step into the boots of planetary mission commanders. The tool accurately simulates survival logistics on Mars (Jezero Crater / Ares Expedition) and the Moon (Artemis Base Alpha). Powered by a real-time mathematical engine, the simulator tracks crew consumables (O2, water, calories, power) based on authentic NASA Life Support (ECLSS) closed-loop models, Sabatier water recovery, and diurnal Sol cycles (24.6h). Users must manage energy grids, deploy research modules, and navigate dynamic Martian dust storms and system emergencies.

2. Benefits & Intended Impact

Complex aerospace engineering is often taught through abstract formulas that can feel inaccessible to young learners. Our project bridges this gap by turning high-stakes space science into an intuitive, gamified experience. Students learn systems engineering, thermodynamic trade-offs, and In-Situ Resource Utilization (ISRU) through direct decision-making. The intended impact is to spark a lasting passion in the Artemis Generation for careers in aerospace, robotics, and STEM. Because the platform requires no downloads or expensive hardware, it can be seamlessly integrated into science classrooms and community learning centers worldwide for free.

3. Tools, Coding Languages, and Software Used

- Architecture & Frontend: Clean HTML5, CSS3 (Mission Control HUD with modern glassmorphism), and Vanilla JavaScript (ES6+ modular state machines).

- Visuals & Audio: HTML5 Canvas API for dynamic Mars terrain generation and particulate dust storms; Web Audio API utilizing synthetic acoustic spectra modeled after NASA InSight and Perseverance wind recordings.

- Scientific Data Integration: Telemetry and standards drawn directly from the NASA Planetary Data System (PDS), Mars 2020 mission archives, and NASA Human Research Program (HRP) metabolic baselines.

- Deployment: Fully public, zero-latency cloud hosting via Tiiny Host.

4. Creativity & Innovation

Unlike conventional space games that rely on fictional sci-fi tropes, our tool combines rigorous, authentic NASA data with creative interactive design. Key innovations include:

- Comparative Planetary Portal: Allows users to dynamically contrast the harsh vacuum and 0.166g gravity of the Moon against the 610 Pa CO2 atmosphere and 0.38g gravity of Mars.

- Authentic NASA R&D Tech Tree: Users research actual flight-tested NASA innovations—such as the MOXIE solid-oxide oxygen generator, Kilopower (KRUSTY) surface nuclear fission, and VIPER volatiles extraction—instead of arbitrary game power-ups.

5. Key Factors Considered by Our Team

- Universal Accessibility: Engineered as a lightweight, zero-install web application that runs smoothly on standard school Chromebooks, laptops, and tablets without requiring passwords or logins.

- Playability vs. Scientific Rigor: We carefully calibrated real NASA metrics (0.84 kg O2, 3.0 L water/day) into intuitive telemetry gauges so younger users grasp system dependencies without being overwhelmed by calculus.

- Educational Reinforcement: Embedded historical NASA context (such as the 2018 Opportunity dust storm) inside procedural events, accompanied by an interactive Astronaut Qualification Exam and achievement badges to reward scientific curiosity.
